body.objective: Students will be able to identify a need in my school or community.
body.iCan: I can identify a need in my school or community.
successCriteria: I can identify a real need in my school or community
I can research users with a survey or interview
I can write a clear problem statement
body.hook: The best inventions don't start with a cool idea; they start with a real problem someone has. Companies spend millions finding out what people actually need. You can do the same thing in your own school, with a survey and some careful listening.

study.title: Find the Real Problem
study.question: How do designers find problems worth solving?
study.passage:
Step 1, Observe (10 minutes): In pairs, walk through part of the school (cafeteria, hallways, library, gym, bus line) and note anything that seems frustrating, slow or confusing.
Step 2, Choose a need (5 minutes): Choose one possible need, such as "Students wait too long in the cafeteria line" or "Lost-and-found items never get returned."
Step 3, Research users (20 minutes): Write a 5-question survey and 3 interview questions. Good questions are open and don't lead people.
• Leading: "Don't you hate the slow lunch line?"
• Better: "Describe your experience in the lunch line."
Survey at least 10 students and interview 2.
Step 4, Check assumptions (5 minutes): What did you assume before? Did your research support it or change it?
Step 5, Problem statement (10 minutes): Use the frame: "[User] needs a way to [need] because [insight from research]."
Example: "Grade 7 students need a faster way to get lunch because 7 of 10 surveyed said they have less than 15 minutes to eat after waiting in line."
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Write and run a survey and interviews

discussion: What need did you choose, and why?
Did your research support or change your assumptions?
Which question gave the most useful answer?
How does your problem statement use evidence?
study.product: Write a one-page needs report: the area observed, survey and interview questions, a summary of results, the assumption you tested and a final problem statement.

examples.title: Leading questions
examples.answer: "How would you describe the noise level in the library?"
examples.explore: Why do leading questions give bad data?

examples.title: Problem statement
examples.problem: Write a problem statement for lost-and-found.
examples.answer: "Students need a way to find lost items quickly because most items are never claimed."
examples.explore: What evidence would make it stronger?

examples.title: Assumptions
examples.problem: You assumed everyone hates the lunch line, but 6 of 10 say it's fine. What now?
examples.answer: Refocus on the 4 who struggle, or choose a different need

examples.title: Survey vs interview
examples.problem: When is an interview better than a survey?
examples.answer: When you need detailed stories and reasons
